claim: Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) is expressed in mammalian photoreceptors.
source: In control retinas, Syt1 immunoreactivity was evident in both rod and cone terminals in the outer plexiform layer (OPL) (Figure 1D), consistent with previous studies (Berntson and Morgans, 2003; Fox and Sanes, 2007; von Kriegstein and Schmitz, 2003).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1D and cited previous studies.

claim: Amphibian photoreceptors do not express Syt1.
source: immunohistochemical studies suggest that mammalian photoreceptors express Syt1, the Ca2+ sensor used at many conventional synapses, but amphibian photoreceptors do not (Berntson and Morgans, 2003; Fox and Sanes, 2007; Heidelberger et al., 2003; Ullrich et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous immunohistochemical studies.

claim: Syt2 is absent from both amphibian and mammalian photoreceptors.
source: Syt2 is absent from both amphibian and mammalian photoreceptors.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: Mice lacking Syt1 die within 48 hr of birth.
source: Mice lacking Syt1 die within 48 hr of birth (Geppert et al., 1994)
evidence: Supported by citation to Geppert et al., 1994.

claim: The retina is not fully developed until P14 in mice.
source: Mice lacking Syt1 die within 48 hr of birth (Geppert et al., 1994) and the retina is not fully developed until P14.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about mouse retinal development.

claim: A conditional Syt1 knockout mouse line was generated with LoxP sites flanking exon 6 of Syt1.
source: To probe the potential function of Syt1 in mouse photoreceptors, we therefore generated a conditional, Cre-dependent Syt1 knockout mouse line with LoxP sites flanking exon 6 of Syt1 (Quadros et al., 2017) (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by citation and Figure 1A-B showing the genetic construct.

claim: Syt1 expression was completely absent from rod spherules in RodSyt1CKO retinas.
source: In contrast to control retinas, Rho-iCre; Syt1flox/flox homozygous mutant (hereafter called RodSyt1CKO) retinas exhibited robust Syt1 expression in cone terminals but Syt1 was completely absent from rod spherules (Figure 1D, middle).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 1D.

claim: Syt1 was absent from cone terminals in ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
source: Conversely, in HRGP-Cre; Syt1flox/flox homozygous mutant (hereafter called ConeSyt1CKO) retinas, Syt1 was absent from cone terminals but strongly expressed in rod spherules (Figure 1D, right).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 1D.

claim: Removal of Syt1 from photoreceptors diminishes ERG b-waves.
source: We first examined the functional impact of the absence of Syt1 from rods and cones by evaluating light-evoked ERG responses using an ex vivo eyecup preparation (Newman and Bartosch, 1999). We focused on the ERG a-wave, a negatively-polarized wave that reflects the hyperpolarizing light responses of rod and cone photoreceptors, and the b-wave, a positively-polarized wave that reflects the depolarization of ON bipolar cells arising from the light-evoked cessation of tonic glutamate release from photoreceptors.
evidence: Supported by ERG data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: RodSyt1CKO retinas exhibited markedly diminished or no b-wave activity at the dimmest flash intensities.
source: RodSyt1CKO retinas, in which rods lack Syt1, exhibited markedly diminished or no b-wave activity at the dimmest flash intensities; a much higher flash intensity was required for RodSyt1CKO b-waves to become significantly non-zero (p>0.05 at intensities below 10−3 of maximum; Figure 2B, maroon data).
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: ConeSyt1CKO retinas exhibited rod-mediated b-waves at low intensities that were as sensitive as controls.
source: Conversely, ConeSyt1CKO retinas exhibited rod-mediated b-waves at low intensities that were as sensitive as controls; the threshold for b-wave detection was the same as controls (10−5 of maximum intensity; p=0.004; Figure 2B, blue data).
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: B-wave amplitudes from ConeSyt1CKO retinas did not increase to the amplitude of control b-waves when evoked by higher intensity flashes.
source: However, b-wave amplitudes from ConeSyt1CKO retinas did not increase to the amplitude of control b-waves when evoked by higher intensity flashes, suggesting a diminished cone contribution to b-waves in ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
evidence: Inferred from ERG data in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no reduction in a-waves of RodSyt1CKO or ConeSyt1CKO retinas throughout the response range.
source: While the b-waves were reduced, there was no reduction in a-waves of RodSyt1CKO or ConeSyt1CKO retinas throughout the response range (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG a-wave measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Isolated photoreceptor responses did not differ significantly between control and RodSyt1CKO retinas.
source: There was a significant variation of responses by light intensity as expected (2-way ANOVA, p<0.0001) but not by genotype (p=0.095). There was also no significant interaction between intensity and genotype (i.e., light did not affect the genotypes differently, p=0.25).
evidence: Demonstrated by isolated photoreceptor responses shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: Diminished photoresponses were not responsible for the marked b-wave reductions in RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
source: These results indicate that diminished photoresponses were not responsible for the marked b-wave reductions in RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that a-waves and isolated photoreceptor responses were normal.

claim: RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO retinas were both significantly less efficient than controls at translating light-evoked Vm changes into neurotransmission changes.
source: At the brightest three intensities where a- and b-waves were reliably attained, RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO retinas were both significantly less efficient than controls at two of the three intensities, suggesting that RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO retinas both exhibited less tonic glutamate release in darkness (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by b-wave/a-wave ratio analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: RodSyt1CKO b-wave2/b-wave1 ratios were increased significantly relative to control retinas at all intensities.
source: Consistent with these predictions, RodSyt1CKO b-wave2/b-wave1 ratios were increased significantly and ConeSyt1CKO b-wave2/b-wave1 ratios were decreased significantly relative to control retinas at all intensities (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by double-flash ERG protocol data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: ConeSyt1CKO b-wave2/b-wave1 ratios were decreased significantly relative to control retinas at all intensities.
source: Consistent with these predictions, RodSyt1CKO b-wave2/b-wave1 ratios were increased significantly and ConeSyt1CKO b-wave2/b-wave1 ratios were decreased significantly relative to control retinas at all intensities (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by double-flash ERG protocol data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: The degree of a-wave desensitization did not differ among control, RodSyt1CKO, and ConeSyt1CKO groups.
source: The degree of a-wave desensitization did not differ among the three groups, supporting the finding that phototransduction is normal in photoreceptors that lack Syt1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by a-wave2/a-wave1 ratio analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: B-waves evoked by the second bright flash in ConeSyt1CKO retinas were nearly undetectable.
source: B-waves evoked by the second bright flash of the double flash protocol in ConeSyt1CKO retinas were nearly undetectable (Figure 3C), suggesting that synaptic output from cones lacking Syt1 was abolished.
evidence: Demonstrated by double-flash ERG data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ERGs from control mice were able to follow 25 Hz flickering stimuli, but ERGs from ConeSyt1CKO retinas were not.
source: ERGs from control mice were able to follow 25 Hz flickering stimuli, but ERGs from ConeSyt1CKO retinas were not (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by flicker ERG data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The absence of any detectable flicker response provides further evidence that release from cones was eliminated by the loss of Syt1 in ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
source: The absence of any detectable flicker response provides further evidence that release from cones was eliminated by the loss of Syt1 in ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
evidence: Inferred from the flicker ERG results in Figure 3E.

claim: Syt1 is required for continuous exocytosis from photoreceptors in darkness.
source: Together, the results in Figure 2 and Figure 3 demonstrate that Syt1 is required for continuous exocytosis from photoreceptors in darkness.
evidence: Inferred from the combined ERG results in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Depolarizing steps produced a robust inward ICa in both control and Syt1-deficient cones.
source: Depolarizing steps produced a robust inward ICa in both control and Syt1-deficient cones, and immediately following ICa activation, ICa in control cones—but not cones lacking Syt1—exhibited a transient outward deflection similar to the vesicular proton-mediated inhibition of ICa described previously in cones and bipolar cells (DeVries, 2001; Palmer et al., 2003) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 4B with citations to previous studies.

claim: ICa in control cones exhibited a transient outward deflection immediately following ICa activation, but cones lacking Syt1 did not.
source: Depolarizing steps produced a robust inward ICa in both control and Syt1-deficient cones, and immediately following ICa activation, ICa in control cones—but not cones lacking Syt1—exhibited a transient outward deflection similar to the vesicular proton-mediated inhibition of ICa described previously in cones and bipolar cells (DeVries, 2001; Palmer et al., 2003) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Buffering the extracellular solution with 20 mM HEPES eliminated ICa inhibition in control cones.
source: To confirm that the transient inhibition of ICa in control cones was mediated by H+, buffering of the extracellular solution was strongly increased with 20 mM HEPES, which eliminated ICa inhibition (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental manipulation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ICa inhibition was evident in control cones during the first step but not during the second step of a paired-pulse protocol.
source: ICa inhibition was evident in control cones during the first step but not during the second step when the pool of releasable vesicles had been depleted (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by paired-pulse protocol data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The transient inhibition of ICa during depolarizing steps in control cones was due to acidification of the cleft upon the release of presynaptic vesicles.
source: Together, these results confirmed that the transient inhibition of ICa during depolarizing steps in control cones was due to acidification of the cleft upon the release of presynaptic vesicles.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of HEPES buffering and paired-pulse experiments.

claim: Iinhibition was undetectable in all cones that lacked Syt1.
source: While the size of Iinhibition averaged 23.5 pA in control cones, Iinhibiton was undetectable in all cones that lacked Syt1 (Figure 4F), indicating that Syt1 is necessary for evoked exocytosis in cones.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of Iinhibition shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Syt1 is necessary for evoked exocytosis in cones.
source: While the size of Iinhibition averaged 23.5 pA in control cones, Iinhibiton was undetectable in all cones that lacked Syt1 (Figure 4F), indicating that Syt1 is necessary for evoked exocytosis in cones.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of Iinhibition in Syt1-deficient cones.

claim: Control cones exhibited inward IA(Glu) tail currents in response to depolarizing steps of 2, 5, and 25 ms duration.
source: Control cones exhibited inward IA(Glu) tail currents in response to depolarizing steps to −10 mV of 2, 5, and 25 ms duration (Figure 5A–C,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: The glutamate transport inhibitor TBOA inhibited IA(Glu) in control cones.
source: The glutamate transport inhibitor TBOA (100 µM) inhibited IA(Glu), demonstrating that these tail currents were generated by presynaptic glutamate transporter activity (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: IA(Glu) was eliminated at all three stimulus durations in Syt1-deficient cones from ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
source: Consistent with earlier results suggesting a complete loss of release from cones, IA(Glu) was eliminated at all three stimulus durations in Syt1-deficient cones from ConeSyt1CKO retinas (Figure 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by IA(Glu) recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Control rods exhibited inward IA(Glu) tail currents in response to steps of 5 and 25 ms duration.
source: Control rods exhibited inward IA(Glu) tail currents in response to steps to −10 mV of 5 and 25 ms duration (Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: IA(Glu) was eliminated in Syt1-deficient rods from RodSyt1CKO retinas when stimulated with a 5 ms test step.
source: In agreement with results from cones, IA(Glu) was eliminated in Syt1-deficient rods from RodSyt1CKO retinas when stimulated with a 5 ms test step.
evidence: Demonstrated by IA(Glu) recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: Some rods lacking Syt1 appeared capable of exocytosis that generated IA(Glu) when stimulated by 25 ms depolarizing steps.
source: However, unlike cones, some rods lacking Syt1 appeared capable of exocytosis that generated IA(Glu) when stimulated by 25 ms depolarizing steps (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by IA(Glu) recordings shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: TBOA inhibited IA(Glu) in RodSyt1CKO rods evoked by 5 and 25 ms steps.
source: TBOA inhibited IA(Glu) in RodSyt1CKO rods evoked by 5 and 25 ms steps (Figure 6C–D), indicating that these currents were due to activation of glutamate transporters.
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Syt1 mediates fast, phasic release evoked by brief elevations of Ca2+ in both rods and cones.
source: Together, these results suggest that Syt1 mediates fast, phasic release evoked by brief elevations of Ca2+ in both rods and cones.
evidence: Inferred from the combined IA(Glu) results in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Syt1 appears to mediate all evoked release in cones.
source: While Syt1 appears to mediate all evoked release in cones, other Ca2+ sensors may be capable of stimulating release from rods given a sufficiently high concentration and/or long duration of Ca2+ entry.
evidence: Inferred from the complete absence of IA(Glu) in Syt1-deficient cones.

claim: Other Ca2+ sensors may be capable of stimulating release from rods given a sufficiently high concentration and/or long duration of Ca2+ entry.
source: While Syt1 appears to mediate all evoked release in cones, other Ca2+ sensors may be capable of stimulating release from rods given a sufficiently high concentration and/or long duration of Ca2+ entry.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of some IA(Glu) in Syt1-deficient rods with 25 ms stimulation.

claim: Spontaneous fast, monophasic inward currents were observed in both rods and cones when voltage-clamped at −70 mV.
source: In the absence of stimulation, we observed spontaneous fast, monophasic inward currents in both rods and cones when they were voltage-clamped at −70 mV, below the activation threshold for ICa (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Spontaneous IA(Glu) events represent glutamate transporter anion currents activated by spontaneous fusion of vesicles in the recorded photoreceptor.
source: These events represent glutamate transporter anion currents activated by spontaneous fusion of vesicles in the recorded photoreceptor (Cork et al., 2016; Grabner et al., 2015; Hasegawa et al., 2006; Szmajda and Devries, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous IA(Glu) events were blocked by TBOA.
source: Spontaneous IA(Glu) events were blocked by TBOA (n = 9 rods, 8 cones).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological manipulation.

claim: Spontaneous release was not abolished in the absence of Syt1.
source: Unlike evoked release, and consistent with other synapses (Schneggenburger and Rosenmund, 2015), spontaneous release was not abolished in the absence of Syt1.
evidence: Demonstrated by the persistence of spontaneous IA(Glu) events in Syt1-deficient photoreceptors, consistent with cited literature.

claim: Neither the quantal amplitude of spontaneous IA(Glu) events nor the frequency of spontaneous release differed between control and ConeSyt1CKO cones.
source: Neither the quantal amplitude of spontaneous IA(Glu) events nor the frequency of spontaneous release differed between control and ConeSyt1CKO cones (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of spontaneous events shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous release increased significantly in rods from RodSyt1CKO retinas.
source: By contrast, the frequency of spontaneous release increased significantly in rods from RodSyt1CKO retinas (Figure 7B), consistent with the suggested role for Syt1 in clamping spontaneous vesicle fusion that is mediated by a different Ca2+ sensor (Kaeser and Regehr, 2014).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of spontaneous events shown in Figure 7B with statistical analysis and citation.

claim: The quantal amplitude did not differ between control rods and rods lacking Syt1.
source: The quantal amplitude did not differ between control rods and rods lacking Syt1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of spontaneous events shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ICa magnitudes were slightly larger in ConeSyt1CKO cones compared to control cones.
source: ICa and QCa magnitudes were slightly larger in ConeSyt1CKO cones compared to control cones; this difference was statistically significant for ICa but not QCa (Figure 8D).
evidence: Demonstrated by ICa measurements shown in Figure 8D with statistical analysis.

claim: V0.5 values of ICa and QCa in Syt1-deficient cones did not differ significantly from controls but tended to be shifted slightly negative.
source: Voltage at half-maximum (V0.5) values (obtained by fitting voltage-activation relationships with Boltzmann functions) of ICa and QCa in Syt1-deficient cones did not differ significantly from controls but tended to be shifted slightly negative.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of voltage-dependence data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Small differences in ICa amplitude and V0.5 between control and ConeSyt1CKO cones likely arose because control cones were subject to H+-mediated ICa inhibition but ConeSyt1CKO cones were not.
source: Because H+-mediated inhibition of ICa reduces current amplitude and shifts voltage dependence positively (Barnes et al., 1993), these small differences in amplitude and V0.5 likely arose because control cones were subject to H+-mediated ICa inhibition but ConeSyt1CKO cones were not (Figure 4).
evidence: Inferred from the known effects of H+ on ICa and the results in Figure 4, with citation.

claim: The amplitude of ICa measured using voltage ramps did not differ between control and Syt1-deficient rods.
source: The amplitude of ICa measured using voltage ramps did not differ between control and Syt1-deficient rods, and the two genotypes did not appear to differ in voltage dependence (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by ICa measurements shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: The marked neurotransmission defects in photoreceptors lacking Syt1 were not due to a reduction in presynaptic Ca2+ influx.
source: These results confirm that the marked neurotransmission defects in photoreceptors lacking Syt1 were not due to a reduction in presynaptic Ca2+ influx.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that ICa was not reduced in Syt1-deficient photoreceptors.

claim: TEM images showed that rods of both control and RodSyt1CKO genotypes contained well-formed synaptic ribbons anchored at the base of rod spherules.
source: TEM images of the OPL from 5 week old control and RodSyt1CKO retinas showed that rods of both genotypes contained well-formed synaptic ribbons anchored at the base of rod spherules with close apposition of the canonical triad of invaginating postsynaptic elements (presumably a central rod bipolar cell dendrite and horizontal cell dendrites on either side of the ribbon, Figure 9A).
evidence: Demonstrated by TEM images shown in Figure 9A.

claim: A dense cloud of vesicles, some of which were tethered to ribbons, surrounded rod ribbons in both control and RodSyt1CKO retinas.
source: A dense cloud of vesicles, some of which were tethered to ribbons, surrounded rod ribbons.
evidence: Observed in TEM images shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Control and Syt1-deficient rod ribbons were approximately equal in size and both exhibited the stereotypical horseshoe shape.
source: IHC experiments showed that control and Syt1-deficient rod ribbons were approximately equal in size and both exhibited the stereotypical horseshoe shape.
evidence: Observed in immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: Cone ribbons in ConeSyt1CKO retinas appeared unchanged.
source: Cone ribbons in ConeSyt1CKO retinas also appeared unchanged (Figure 9B).
evidence: Observed in immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Rods and cones lacking Syt1 maintained clusters of CaV1.4 channels below their ribbons.
source: Consistent with the finding that ICa was undiminished in the absence of Syt1, rods and cones lacking Syt1 maintained clusters of CaV1.4 channels below their ribbons (Figure 9B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Measurements of the thickness of the ONL, OPL, and INL did not differ among RodSyt1CKO, ConeSyt1CKO, and their respective littermate control retinas.
source: Measurements of the thickness of the ONL, OPL, and INL from IHC images did not differ among RodSyt1CKO, ConeSyt1CKO, and their respective littermate control retinas (Figure 9C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The density of cone terminals in the OPL did not differ between ConeSyt1CKO and control.
source: Furthermore, the density of cone terminals in the OPL, assessed by counting tdTomato-positive cone terminals in flatmount retinas, did not differ between ConeSyt1CKO and control (Figure 9D).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 9D.

claim: There was no evidence for sprouting of dendrites or an increase of ectopic synapses in the ONL in RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
source: We compared the anatomy of horizontal cell and bipolar cell dendrites in control, RodSyt1CKO, and ConeSyt1CKO retinas and found no evidence for sprouting of dendrites or an increase of ectopic synapses in the ONL.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 10-12.

claim: Postsynaptic elements continued to make proper contacts with rod and cone ribbons in the OPL whether or not Syt1 was present in the associated presynaptic terminals.
source: Triple labeling with antibodies to CtBP2 (to label ribbons), Syt1, and calbindin (to label horizontal cells, Figure 10) or secretagogin (to label cone bipolar cells, Figure 11); and double labeling of ribbons (with antibodies to CtBP2) and rod bipolar cells (with antibodies to PKCα, Figure 12) demonstrated that postsynaptic elements continued to make proper contacts with rod and cone ribbons in the OPL whether or not Syt1 was present in the associated presynaptic terminals.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 10-12.

claim: Photoreceptor synapses of 10-week-old RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO mice also appeared unchanged.
source: While we focused on mice 4–6 weeks of age, photoreceptor synapses of 10-week-old RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO mice also appeared unchanged (data not shown).
evidence: Stated observation from additional experiments.

claim: Both rod and cone synapses develop and are maintained normally in RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO mice.
source: These results revealed that both rod and cone synapses develop and are maintained normally in RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO mice, suggesting that neither Syt1-mediated activity nor Syt1 itself are required for establishing or maintaining photoreceptor ribbon structures or their contact with postsynaptic neurons, even weeks after synaptic maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined anatomical results in Figures 9-12.

claim: Neither Syt1-mediated activity nor Syt1 itself are required for establishing or maintaining photoreceptor ribbon structures or their contact with postsynaptic neurons.
source: These results revealed that both rod and cone synapses develop and are maintained normally in RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO mice, suggesting that neither Syt1-mediated activity nor Syt1 itself are required for establishing or maintaining photoreceptor ribbon structures or their contact with postsynaptic neurons, even weeks after synaptic maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the normal synaptic anatomy in Syt1-deficient photoreceptors.

claim: Syt1 is the major Ca2+ sensor linking presynaptic Ca2+ and vesicular exocytosis at photoreceptor synaptic ribbon active zones.
source: Our data demonstrate that Syt1 is the major Ca2+ sensor linking presynaptic Ca2+ and vesicular exocytosis at photoreceptor synaptic ribbon active zones.
evidence: Inferred from the combined functional results showing marked reduction in release without Syt1.

claim: In both rods and cones, Syt1 appears to mediate fast, synchronous release evoked by brief depolarizing stimuli.
source: In both rods and cones, Syt1 appears to mediate fast, synchronous release evoked by brief depolarizing stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the elimination of fast IA(Glu) responses in Syt1-deficient photoreceptors.

claim: Syt1 mediates continuous release in darkness in both rods and cones.
source: Because the ERG b-wave reflects ON bipolar cell light responses, suppression of the b-wave without changes in the a-wave or photoreceptor ICa in RodSyt1CKO and ConeSyt1CKO retinas suggests that Syt1 also mediates continuous release in darkness in both rods and cones.
evidence: Inferred from the ERG results showing reduced b-waves without changes in a-waves.

claim: Rods may be capable of some slow, Syt1-independent evoked release.
source: The persistence of IA(Glu) evoked by 25 ms steps in rods lacking Syt1 suggests they may be capable of some slow, Syt1-independent evoked release.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of IA(Glu) in Syt1-deficient rods with longer stimulation.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous miniature release events increased in rods lacking Syt1, consistent with Syt1 functioning as a clamp of spontaneous fusion.
source: Consistent with other synapses where Syt1 has been shown to inhibit spontaneous fusion of vesicles (Kavalali, 2015), the frequency of spontaneous miniature release events increased in rods lacking Syt1 (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by spontaneous event analysis in Figure 7 with citation.

claim: Syt1-deficient cones did not exhibit an increase in spontaneous release frequency, suggesting that interactions between Syt1 and other exocytotic proteins differ in rods and cones.
source: Syt1-deficient cones did not exhibit a similar increase in frequency suggesting that interactions between Syt1 and other exocytotic proteins differ in rods and cones.
evidence: Inferred from the different effects on spontaneous release frequency in rods vs. cones.

claim: Photoreceptors utilize synaptic ribbons to sustain continuous exocytosis while making rapid, fine adjustments to release rate.
source: To encode light-dependent changes in membrane potential, rod and cone photoreceptors utilize synaptic ribbons to sustain continuous exocytosis while making rapid, fine adjustments to release rate.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about photoreceptor function.

claim: Release kinetics are shaped by vesicle delivery down ribbons and by properties of exocytotic Ca2+ sensors.
source: Release kinetics are shaped by vesicle delivery down ribbons and by properties of exocytotic Ca2+ sensors.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about ribbon synapse function.

claim: Photoreceptors lacking Syt1 exhibited marked reductions in exocytosis as measured by electroretinography and single-cell recordings.
source: Photoreceptors lacking Syt1 exhibited marked reductions in exocytosis as measured by electroretinography and single-cell recordings.
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG and single-cell recording data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Syt1 did not alter synaptic anatomy or reduce Ca2+ currents.
source: Loss of Syt1 did not alter synaptic anatomy or reduce Ca2+ currents.
evidence: Demonstrated by anatomical and electrophysiological data in Figures 8-12.

claim: Syt1 mediates both phasic and tonic release at photoreceptor synapses.
source: These results suggest that Syt1 mediates both phasic and tonic release at photoreceptor synapses, revealing unexpected flexibility in the ability of Syt1 to regulate Ca2+-dependent synaptic transmission.
evidence: Inferred from the combined functional results showing Syt1 mediates both fast and continuous release.

claim: The membrane potential of photoreceptors in darkness is relatively depolarized.
source: The membrane potential of photoreceptors in darkness is relatively depolarized, allowing Ca2+ to enter the cell continuously through voltage-gated CaV1.4 Ca2+ channels clustered beneath ribbon-style active zones.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about photoreceptor physiology.

claim: Ca2+ entry through CaV1.4 channels stimulates continuous Ca2+-dependent exocytosis of glutamate-filled vesicles in darkness.
source: The membrane potential of photoreceptors in darkness is relatively depolarized, allowing Ca2+ to enter the cell continuously through voltage-gated CaV1.4 Ca2+ channels clustered beneath ribbon-style active zones. This in turn stimulates continuous Ca2+-dependent exocytosis of glutamate-filled vesicles (LoGiudice and Matthews, 2009; Mercer and Thoreson, 2011; Pangrsic et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Absorption of photons causes photoreceptors to hyperpolarize, thereby reducing Ca2+ influx and the rate of exocytosis.
source: Absorption of photons in the photoreceptor outer segment causes photoreceptors to hyperpolarize, thereby reducing Ca2+ influx and the rate of exocytosis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about photoreceptor physiology.

claim: Various vesicular Ca2+-sensing proteins including synaptotagmin, otoferlin, and Doc2 are capable of mediating exocytosis in different neurons.
source: Various vesicular Ca2+-sensing proteins including synaptotagmin (Syt), otoferlin, and Doc2 are capable of mediating exocytosis in different neurons (Kaeser and Regehr, 2014; Pang and Südhof, 2010; Pangršič et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Different kinetic phases of exocytosis can be shaped by properties of the Ca2+ sensor mediating release.
source: Different kinetic phases of exocytosis can be shaped by properties of the Ca2+ sensor mediating release.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about synaptic transmission.

claim: At many synapses, fast synchronous, slow asynchronous, and spontaneous modes of release utilize distinct Ca2+ sensors with differing Ca2+ binding properties.
source: At many synapses, fast synchronous, slow asynchronous, and spontaneous modes of release utilize distinct Ca2+ sensors with differing Ca2+ binding properties (Kaeser and Regehr, 2014).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Fast phasic release evoked by brief depolarization is typically mediated by Syt1 or the closely-related Syt2.
source: Fast phasic release evoked by brief depolarization is typically mediated by Syt1 or the closely-related Syt2 (Augustine and Charlton, 1986; Bollmann et al., 2000; Dodge and Rahamimoff, 1967; Jarsky et al., 2010; Landò and Zucker, 1994; Schneggenburger and Neher, 2000).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Syt7 has been suggested to mediate a slow, asynchronous phase of release that follows the initial fast burst of release.
source: Syt7 has been suggested to mediate a slow, asynchronous phase of release that follows the initial fast burst of release (Bacaj et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2015; Turecek and Regehr, 2018; Wen et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Doc2 has been proposed as a sensor for both asynchronous and spontaneous release.
source: Doc2 has been proposed as a sensor for both asynchronous and spontaneous release (Groffen et al., 2010; Pang et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Rod and cone photoreceptors are capable of fast and slow phases of depolarization-evoked release as well as spontaneous release.
source: Rod and cone photoreceptors are capable of fast and slow phases of depolarization-evoked release as well as spontaneous release (Cadetti et al., 2005; DeVries and Schwartz, 1999; Rabl et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: At ribbon synapses, the kinetics of release can be shaped not only by properties of the sensor molecules but also by the rate at which vesicles are delivered to release sites at the base of the ribbon.
source: At ribbon synapses, the kinetics of release can be shaped not only by properties of the sensor molecules but also by the rate at which vesicles are delivered to release sites at the base of the ribbon (Jackman et al., 2009; Matthews and Fuchs, 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: In cone photoreceptors, the initial fast phase of release matches the number of vesicles in the readily releasable pool that are tethered at the base of the ribbon in contact with the adjacent plasma membrane.
source: In cone photoreceptors, the initial fast phase of release matches the number of vesicles in the readily releasable pool that are tethered at the base of the ribbon in contact with the adjacent plasma membrane (Bartoletti et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Sustained depolarization stimulates a second phase of release that matches the number of vesicles attached to the remainder of the ribbon.
source: Sustained depolarization stimulates a second phase of release that matches the number of vesicles attached to the remainder of the ribbon, suggesting that this slower phase reflects release of vesicles that have descended to re-occupy vacant release sites at the ribbon base.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation (Bartoletti et al., 2010).

claim: After depleting ribbon-attached vesicles, release from cones can be maintained indefinitely at a linear rate, presumably reflecting replenishment of the ribbon by cytoplasmic vesicles.
source: After depleting these two pools of ribbon-attached vesicles, release from cones can be maintained indefinitely at a linear rate, presumably reflecting replenishment of the ribbon by cytoplasmic vesicles (Bartoletti et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation and speculation about mechanism.

claim: Ribbon-mediated release from rods appears to utilize similar mechanisms to cones.
source: Ribbon-mediated release from rods appears to utilize similar mechanisms (Li et al., 2010; Van Hook and Thoreson, 2015)
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Rods are capable of slow release at non-ribbon release sites that may be analogous to asynchronous release at conventional synapses.
source: but rods are also capable of slow release at non-ribbon release sites that may be analogous to asynchronous release at conventional synapses (Babai et al., 2010; Cadetti et al., 2006; Suryanarayanan and Slaughter, 2006).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations and speculation.

claim: The identity of the molecular Ca2+ sensors that mediate different forms of release in photoreceptors is unknown.
source: The identity of the molecular Ca2+ sensors that mediate different forms of release in photoreceptors is unknown.
evidence: Stated as a gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: Exocytosis from amphibian photoreceptor synapses shows an unusually high Ca2+ affinity and shallow Ca2+ cooperativity.
source: Unlike release from bipolar cells and most other neurons, exocytosis from amphibian photoreceptor synapses shows an unusually high Ca2+ affinity and shallow Ca2+ cooperativity, suggesting photoreceptors may employ an unusual Ca2+ sensor (Duncan et al., 2010; Rabl et al., 2005; Rieke and Schwartz, 1996; Thoreson et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Many properties of release are similar in mammalian and amphibian photoreceptors.
source: Many properties of release are similar in mammals and amphibians
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: A single sensor, Syt1, mediates sustained and phasic release from rods and cones.
source: Electroretinography (ERG) experiments and single-cell recordings from rods and cones indicate that a single sensor, Syt1, mediates sustained and phasic release from rods and cones.
evidence: Inferred from the combined ERG and single-cell recording results.

claim: Other Ca2+ sensors may be involved in mediating some slow release from rods and spontaneous release from both rods and cones.
source: Other Ca2+ sensors may be involved in mediating some slow release from rods and spontaneous release from both rods and cones.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of some slow release in rods and spontaneous release in both cell types.

claim: Syt1 functions as a clamp of spontaneous fusion at many synapses.
source: Consistent with other synapses where Syt1 has been shown to inhibit spontaneous fusion of vesicles (Kavalali, 2015)
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Doc2 may trigger spontaneous release.
source: This result supports the hypothesis that Syt1 functions as a clamp of spontaneous fusion and that another Ca2+ sensor, perhaps Doc2, triggers spontaneous release (Courtney et al., 2018; Groffen et al., 2010).
evidence: Speculation based on literature citations.

claim: Interactions between Syt1 and other exocytotic proteins differ in rods and cones.
source: Syt1-deficient cones did not exhibit a similar increase in frequency suggesting that interactions between Syt1 and other exocytotic proteins differ in rods and cones.
evidence: Inferred from the different effects on spontaneous release frequency.

claim: Ca2+ sensors other than Syt1 may be able to trigger release from rods given sufficient Ca2+ concentration and duration.
source: Alternatively, Ca2+ sensors other than Syt1 may be able to trigger release given a sufficient Ca2+ concentration and duration. Possible candidates include Doc2 and Syt7, which have both been suggested to mediate asynchronous release from neurons (Bacaj et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2015; Turecek and Regehr, 2018; Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculation based on the persistence of some release in Syt1-deficient rods and literature citations.

claim: The exocytotic Ca2+ sensor in amphibian photoreceptors shows a Ca2+ cooperativity of n = 2–3.
source: The exocytotic Ca2+ sensor in amphibian photoreceptors shows a higher Ca2+ affinity and lower Ca2+ cooperativity (n = 2–3) than most other synapses (Duncan et al., 2010; Rabl et al., 2003; Rieke and Schwartz, 1996).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Syt4 does not bind Ca2+ ions but imparts a linear Ca2+ dependence to release from mature hair cells involving otoferlin.
source: Syt4 does not bind Ca2+ ions but nevertheless imparts a linear Ca2+ dependence to release from mature hair cells that involves the protein otoferlin with six Ca2+-binding sites (Cho et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Interactions between Syt1 and other SNARE complex members and intracellular signaling pathways can influence Ca2+ cooperativity.
source: Interactions between Syt1 and other SNARE complex members and intracellular signaling pathways have also been shown to influence cooperativity (Sørensen et al., 2002; Stewart et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: At conventional synapses, different kinetic components of exocytosis often involve the use of different Ca2+ sensors.
source: Conventional and ribbon synapses both exhibit fast and slow components to exocytosis. At conventional synapses, these different kinetic components often involve the use of different Ca2+ sensors, such as Syt1 or Syt2 for fast release and Syt7 or Doc2 for slow release (Bacaj et al., 2013; Jarsky et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Kinetics of fast and slow release at bipolar and photoreceptor ribbon synapses are thought to be limited by the speed at which vesicles can be delivered to release sites at the base of the ribbon.
source: At ribbon synapses, kinetics of fast and slow release at bipolar and photoreceptor ribbon synapses are thought to be limited by the speed at which vesicles can be delivered to release sites at the base of the ribbon, which would not require different Ca2+ sensors to mediate fast and slow release (Bartoletti et al., 2010; Sterling and Matthews, 2005).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Release at mature ribbon synapses of cochlear hair cells appears to involve only a single sensor, otoferlin, and not Syt1, Syt2 or Syt7.
source: Consistent with this, release at mature ribbon synapses of cochlear hair cells appears to involve only a single sensor, otoferlin, and not Syt1, Syt2 or Syt7 (Beurg et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Syt1 appears to mediate fast release from bipolar cell ribbon synapses while Syt7 contributes to slow asynchronous release.
source: On the other hand, like conventional synapses, Syt1 appears to mediate fast release from bipolar cell ribbon synapses while Syt7 contributes to slow asynchronous release (Luo et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Both phasic and tonic release in cones occur exclusively at ribbons.
source: In cones, both phasic and tonic release are understood to occur exclusively at ribbons (Jackman et al., 2009; Snellman et al., 2011)
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Syt1-mediated release at ribbons, with kinetics dictated by vesicle delivery, is the dominant mechanism of both fast and slow exocytosis in mouse cones.
source: This suggests that Syt1-mediated release at ribbons, with kinetics dictated by vesicle delivery, is the dominant mechanism of both fast and slow exocytosis in mouse cones.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that all evoked release was eliminated in Syt1-deficient cones.

claim: Fast release from rods uses ribbon-mediated mechanisms similar to cones.
source: Fast release from rods uses ribbon-mediated mechanisms similar to cones (Li et al., 2010; Van Hook and Thoreson, 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Rods are capable of slow non-ribbon release stimulated by Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR) from intracellular ER stores.
source: However, unlike cones, rods are also capable of slow non-ribbon release stimulated by Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR) from intracellular ER stores (Babai et al., 2010; Cadetti et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013; Krizaj et al., 2003; Suryanarayanan and Slaughter, 2006).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Inhibition of CICR significantly reduced light responses of horizontal cells and bipolar cells in amphibian and mouse retina.
source: Inhibition of CICR significantly reduced light responses of horizontal cells and bipolar cells in amphibian and mouse retina, suggesting that non-ribbon release contributes significantly to continuous release from rods in darkness (Babai et al., 2010; Cadetti et al., 2006; Suryanarayanan and Slaughter, 2006).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Deletion of Syt1 eliminated most of the rod-driven b-wave.
source: We found that deletion of Syt1 eliminated most of the rod-driven b-wave and that only a small component of slow release persisted in rods lacking Syt1.
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: If slow asynchronous release from rods employs a sensor other than Syt1, it is not likely to be a major contributor to continuous release in darkness.
source: This suggests that if, like bipolar cells, slow asynchronous release from rods employs a sensor other than Syt1, it is not likely to be a major contributor to continuous release in darkness.
evidence: Inferred from the marked reduction in rod-driven b-waves without Syt1.

claim: The increase in spontaneous release frequency in rods lacking Syt1 might be large enough to obscure light-evoked changes in release mediated by another sensor.
source: However, it is also possible that the increase in spontaneous release frequency in rods lacking Syt1 (Figure 7) might be large enough to obscure light-evoked changes in release mediated by another sensor and thereby block the b-wave.
evidence: Speculation about an alternative explanation for the results.

claim: The use of Syt1 may promote a close temporal association between the formation of Ca2+ nanodomains and vesicle release.
source: The use of Syt1 may promote a close temporal association between the formation of Ca2+ nanodomains and vesicle release (Bartoletti et al., 2011; Van Hook and Thoreson, 2015), even during continuous release in darkness.
evidence: Speculation based on the known properties of Syt1 with citations.

claim: Syt1-deficient photoreceptors exhibit undiminished ICa.
source: Syt1-deficient photoreceptors exhibit undiminished ICa and maintain synaptic contacts with postsynaptic horizontal and bipolar cells despite diminished synaptic communication.
evidence: Demonstrated by ICa measurements in Figure 8.

claim: Syt1-deficient photoreceptors maintain synaptic contacts with postsynaptic horizontal and bipolar cells despite diminished synaptic communication.
source: Syt1-deficient photoreceptors exhibit undiminished ICa and maintain synaptic contacts with postsynaptic horizontal and bipolar cells despite diminished synaptic communication.
evidence: Demonstrated by anatomical data in Figures 9-12.

claim: Photoreceptor synapses were morphologically indistinguishable in control, RodSyt1CKO, and ConeSyt1CKO retinas.
source: Immunohistochemistry and TEM data showed that photoreceptor synapses were morphologically indistinguishable in control, RodSyt1CKO, and ConeSyt1CKO retinas (Figures 9–12).
evidence: Demonstrated by anatomical data in Figures 9-12.

claim: Previous studies of mouse photoreceptors examining mutations or absence of critical ribbon-associated proteins have demonstrated reduced synaptic contacts, malformed ribbons, and/or ectopic photoreceptor synapses.
source: Previous studies of mouse photoreceptors examining mutations or the absence of critical ribbon-associated proteins CaBP4 (Haeseleer et al., 2004), CAST (tom tom Dieck et al., 2012), Bassoon (Specht et al., 2007), and the CaV1.4 channel subunits α1 (Chang et al., 2006; Mansergh et al., 2005), β2 (Ball et al., 2002; Katiyar et al., 2015), and α2δ4 (Wang et al., 2017; Wycisk et al., 2006) have all demonstrated reduced synaptic contacts, malformed ribbons, and/or ectopic photoreceptor synapses with postsynaptic dendritic sprouting into the ONL, with concomitant synaptic transmission defects.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Photoreceptor synaptic dysfunction is the initiating event that causes horizontal cells to sprout ectopic dendrites in retinal degeneration.
source: It has also been suggested that photoreceptor synaptic dysfunction is the initiating event that causes horizontal cells to sprout ectopic dendrites in retinal degeneration (Soto and Kerschensteiner, 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The absence of Syt1 from photoreceptors did not affect the development or maintenance of rod or cone synapses up to 10 postnatal weeks.
source: That the absence of Syt1 from photoreceptors did not affect the development or maintenance (up to 10 postnatal weeks) of rod or cone synapses was surprising given its integral role in photoreceptor neurotransmission.
evidence: Demonstrated by anatomical data showing normal synaptic structure.

claim: Expressing tetanus toxin to silence mouse photoreceptors throughout development caused only subtle morphological changes to photoreceptor ribbons and occasional ectopic sprouting of postsynaptic dendrites.
source: However, consistent with our results, Cao et al. (2015) found that expressing tetanus toxin to silence mouse photoreceptors throughout development caused only subtle morphological changes to photoreceptor ribbons and occasional ectopic sprouting of postsynaptic dendrites without major changes in ONL/OPL architecture.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: When RIBEYE was deleted in mice, neurotransmission was diminished but OPL anatomy was not markedly altered.
source: When the integral ribbon protein RIBEYE was deleted in mice, neurotransmission was diminished but OPL anatomy was not markedly altered (Maxeiner et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Depriving developing mice of visual experience had only a subtle effect on the formation of cone synapses, but not rod synapses.
source: Another study that deprived developing mice of visual experience found only a subtle effect on the formation of cone synapses, but not rod synapses (Dunn et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Mutations of postsynaptic mGluR6 signaling cascade members disrupt communication, but not synaptic anatomy, between photoreceptors and ON bipolar cells.
source: Finally, mutations of postsynaptic mGluR6 signaling cascade members disrupt communication, but not synaptic anatomy, between photoreceptors and ON bipolar cells (McCall and Gregg, 2008).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Ribbon-associated Ca2+ channel complexes, ribbon structural components, trans-synaptic protein interactions, or other Ca2+-dependent processes may be the dominant factors establishing photoreceptor synaptic connectivity.
source: These results support the hypothesis that ribbon-associated Ca2+ channel complexes, ribbon structural components, trans-synaptic protein interactions, or other Ca2+-dependent processes (i.e., as a second messenger) may be the dominant factors establishing photoreceptor synaptic connectivity (Joiner and Lee, 2015; Schmitz, 2009).
evidence: Inferred from the combined results with citations.

claim: Syt1 is a vesicular protein with no direct association with the ribbon complex.
source: Because Syt1 is a vesicular protein with no direct association with the ribbon complex, our results are consistent with previous studies emphasizing the importance of proteins involved in active zone organization while suggesting a limited role for light-evoked neurotransmission in maintaining photoreceptor synapse integrity.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Syt1 localization.

claim: Light-evoked neurotransmission may play a limited role in maintaining photoreceptor synapse integrity.
source: Because Syt1 is a vesicular protein with no direct association with the ribbon complex, our results are consistent with previous studies emphasizing the importance of proteins involved in active zone organization while suggesting a limited role for light-evoked neurotransmission in maintaining photoreceptor synapse integrity.
evidence: Inferred from the normal synaptic anatomy despite loss of Syt1-mediated transmission.

claim: Spontaneous activity plays a key role in synaptogenesis within the retina and throughout the CNS.
source: Spontaneous activity is understood to play a key role in synaptogenesis within the retina and throughout the CNS (Andreae and Burrone, 2018; Soto et al., 2012)
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Ca2+-dependent neurotransmission before eye opening has been implicated in cone-horizontal cell synapse formation.
source: and Ca2+-dependent neurotransmission before eye opening has been implicated in cone-horizontal cell synapse formation specifically (Raven et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Rods and cones lacking Syt1 remained capable of spontaneous release.
source: Rods and cones lacking Syt1 remained capable of spontaneous release (Figure 7), so it is possible that Syt1-independent release is sufficient for both the formation and maintenance of photoreceptor synapses.
evidence: Demonstrated by spontaneous event recordings in Figure 7.

claim: Syt1-independent release may be sufficient for both the formation and maintenance of photoreceptor synapses.
source: Rods and cones lacking Syt1 remained capable of spontaneous release (Figure 7), so it is possible that Syt1-independent release is sufficient for both the formation and maintenance of photoreceptor synapses.
evidence: Speculation based on the persistence of spontaneous release.

claim: Syt1 expression may rise briefly before its Cre-dependent deletion and this may be sufficient to establish photoreceptor wiring.
source: It is also possible that Syt1 expression may rise briefly before its Cre-dependent deletion and this may be sufficient to establish photoreceptor wiring.
evidence: Speculation about an alternative explanation.

claim: Cre expression in both HRGP-Cre and Rho-iCre mice rises in parallel with formation of photoreceptor synapses during the second postnatal week in mouse retina.
source: Cre expression in both HRGP-Cre and Rho-iCre mice (Le et al., 2004; Li et al., 2005) rises in parallel with formation of photoreceptor synapses during the second postnatal week in mouse retina (Blanks et al., 1974).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Subtle morphological changes may have occurred that evaded detection in this study.
source: It is also possible that subtle morphological changes occurred that evaded our detection or that Syt1-deficient photoreceptor synapses could form properly but degenerate at time points beyond those evaluated by our study.
evidence: Speculation about limitations of the study.

claim: Syt1-deficient photoreceptor synapses could form properly but degenerate at time points beyond those evaluated by this study.
source: It is also possible that subtle morphological changes occurred that evaded our detection or that Syt1-deficient photoreceptor synapses could form properly but degenerate at time points beyond those evaluated by our study.
evidence: Speculation about limitations of the study.
